title: How To Never Get Angry And Transform Your Classroom
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Using the comic image of a coconut knocking away a teacher's ability to ever get annoyed at students, Linsin argues that eliminating anger-based reactions to misbehavior entirely — never lecturing, sighing, glaring, or scolding — is one of the most consequential single changes a teacher can make. He lists the predictable payoffs: lower stress, higher likability, real power behind rules and consequences, a tension-free room, more instructional time, no parent complaints, and students who want to behave. His practical method is a short daily ritual done before school: close the door, sit, close your eyes, focus on breathing for 30 seconds, then consciously decide that no matter what happens that day, you will stay calm inside and out. He frames this as remarkably effective despite its simplicity, arguing that with daily repetition it becomes a default personality trait even for naturally nervous people, and stresses it works best as part of the full SCM approach that removes any need to rely on anger in the first place.
points: Eliminating anger-based reactions to misbehavior entirely — no lecturing, sighing, glaring, or scolding — is framed as one of the single most consequential changes a teacher can make.
Use a short pre-school ritual: close the door, sit, close your eyes, breathe for 30 seconds, then consciously decide to stay calm inside and out no matter what happens that day.
The predictable payoffs of never reacting in anger include lower stress, higher likability, real power behind consequences, and more time for learning.
With daily repetition, staying calm can become a default personality trait even for a naturally nervous person outside of school.
The full SCM approach is designed so strategies work together, removing any need or reason to rely on anger-based reactions in the first place.
quotes: What if while on vacation a coconut fell from a tree, bonked you on the head, and took away your ability to get annoyed at your students?
The only thing in your toolkit to curb misbehavior would be your classroom management plan.
Your stress level would plummet. Your likability would skyrocket. Your rules and consequences would have real power.
It does take some discipline, but you only need to set aside a minute or two every morning before school.
Decide that no matter what happens that day—even if a troop of bonobos come swinging through your classroom—you’re going to keep as cool as a morning mist, inside and out.
Keeping your cool will become a habit. It will become your default setting, just who you are.
